title: Money
hookLine: the love of money, not money, is the trouble (1 Timothy 6:10)
tomorrow: what does it cost to buy back an hour?

cards: Two friends get their first real paychecks the same week. One says: enjoy it, it's a gift, you earned it. The other says: careful, money gets its hooks in.
Both of them could open a Bible and find their verse. Christians have argued this one for a very long time: is wealth a blessing, or a danger? Today, let both sides speak.

teach.b: One side reads Proverbs: “The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.” Deuteronomy tells Israel to remember that it's God who gives the power to get wealth. On this view, money is a gift.
Earn it honestly, enjoy it with thanks, use it well, and don't be ashamed of it. The other side reads Mark.
A rich man walks away from Jesus sad, and Jesus says: “How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!”
And in Luke: “Ye cannot serve God and mammon.” Mammon is an old word for wealth, spoken of like a lord who gives orders.

On this view, money is dangerous, and holding it loosely, even giving much of it away, is the safer road. Some Christians have chosen poverty on purpose for exactly this reason. Now notice where they meet.
Proverbs never calls greed a blessing, and Jesus never calls coins evil.

teach.h: THE LOVE OF IT IS THE ROOT.
teach.b: The First Letter to Timothy draws the line both can stand on: “For the love of money is the root of all evil.”
The love of it. So the real question, for both sides, is who's giving the orders.

how: Christians practice giving in different ways: some give a tithe, a tenth, to their church; others give as they're able; some communities of monks, nuns and friars take vows of poverty.

o: the root of every evil thing in the world
a sign that God approves of a person
a tool that can serve good things or rule you

games.q: two sides, one line — tap the pairs.
p: the blessing of the LORD maketh rich
how hardly shall the rich enter
the love of money is the root

s: the Bible says money is the root of all evil
it says the love of money is the root of all evil.
Proverbs links wealth with the blessing of the LORD
the blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.
Jesus says a person can serve God and mammon equally
ye cannot serve God and mammon.

games.q: your friend plans to give most of her earnings away someday, because she thinks wealth is spiritually risky. you lean the other way. what is her best case, in her own terms?
o: Jesus said the rich hardly enter the kingdom; held loosely, money can't rule her.
she probably just feels guilty about having more than other people.
Proverbs says riches are a curse, so she's reading it the plain way.
games.why: her steelman is Mark and Luke: riches can become a master. yours is Proverbs: the blessing of the LORD maketh rich. both sides ask who is in charge.

practice: Take out a card, a bill, or your banking app, and look at it for the sit as if it were someone who works for you.
Bring to mind one spending habit you repeat without thinking, and ask it plainly: are you serving something I love, or giving the orders? If you pray, you can offer the answer to God.

wordCard.voice: Money. A good servant and a demanding master; the trouble is the love of it, not the coins.

orig.note: the Greek word behind 'mammon' in Luke 16:13: wealth, money.

carryVoice: The line to keep: money is a servant, as long as the orders run one way. Until tomorrow.
